# Copper September 2011 

- During a month which has seen strike action by at least three significant-sized copper properties and the promise of some disruption at a fourth, coupled with reports of rising metal imports by the world’s largest consumer, one would ordinarily think that copper prices would have strengthened.  But September has proved to be no ordinary month. Ending August at US$9197/t ($4.17/lb, cash), the omens for copper came quickly: US$100/t lost on the first trading day of September, a further US$50/t on the 2<sup>nd</sup> .  By the Monday (19<sup>th</sup> ), there were no bulls to be found anywhere, and copper’s price fell away with such undignified haste that it made that US$9000/t level look like a mirage. 

- We do not believe that _traditional_ supply-demand metals fundamentals are responsible for this flight of capital away from copper.  In our view, beyond the macro concerns of the global economy, copper (and nickel) took a beating because from one point of view they could absorb it best.  That is, these were the metals whose prices most exceeded their respective marginal costs of production, and there was sufficient scope for a price reduction to take place without threatening the production base from a cost perspective. 

- Movements in both commodity and equity markets have been dramatic over the past month but the extent of real impact on end use demand remains to be seen.  We had always forecast a slowdown in demand in the second half of the year, although we have toned this down further since our last monthly report and now expect global growth of 4.6% this year. 

- The spot concentrate market proved to be far more stable than the metal market over the course of the month, with trader buying terms ($48/t & 4.8c/lb) essentially unchanged on levels seen during August.  That said as we go to press, there are rumours of a spot deal agreement at $35/t & 3.5c/lb.  At the same time declining concentrate stocks in China have contributed to a reduction in buying terms, from $60/t & 6c/lb a month ago, to $45/t & 4.5c/lb currently.

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market Developments 

**September brings the bloodbath…** During a month which

has seen the initiation of strike action by at least three significant-sized copper properties and the promise of some disruption at a fourth, coupled with reports of rising metal imports by the world’s largest consumer, one would ordinarily think that copper prices would have strengthened. Unfortunately, September has proved to be no ordinary month.  Ending August at US$9197/t ($4.17/lb, cash), the omens for copper came quickly: US$100/t lost on the first trading day of September, a further US$50/t on the 2<sup>nd</sup> , another US$65/t fell away the following Monday, and by the 6<sup>th</sup> cash copper was trading at US$8919/t ($4.05/lb).  A fleeting moment of support came on the 7-8<sup>th</sup> of the month as the news headlines turned to the well-aired issues of tightening supply due to a likely strike at Freeport’s Grasberg operations in Indonesia and Cerro Verde complex in Peru.  This lifted prices back above the US$9000/t mark by a hair.  But by the end of that opening full week of the month, the 9<sup>th</sup> , the bears had taken control once again, and for the first time since the fourth quarter of 2010, prices showed signs of being unable to support the psychologically important US$9000/t and $4.00/lb levels any longer. 

**..and copper oozes red** Ending that first week at US$8904/t ($4.04/lb), the writing appeared on the wall as soon as trading opened the following Monday, 12<sup>th</sup> , as another US$250/t from the cash price melted away, now at $8645/t ($3.92/lb).  Market players had read nothing but bad news about the global economy in their weekend papers, but a report out of Chile saying that Codelco’s clients had requested orders to be deferred or cancelled in some cases was also partly responsible.  Again, though, supply-side issues at Freeport’s facilities provided a crutch for prices, and cash copper edged back up over the following four days through to the Friday 16<sup>th</sup> to average US$8742/t ($3.97/lb).  After all, with Grasberg threatening a month-long strike and Cerro Verde now looking at an indefinite strike and thereby removing close to 65kt/m of copper from the market at a time when China was seemingly back in the game, sub-$4/lb copper was beginning to look cheap.  We hear that force majeure has been declared on Grasberg shipments and that operations are being maintained at about one third of capacity using skeleton crews that include miners that have returned to work. 

But then more weekend news supplements came out, and by the next Monday (19<sup>th</sup> ), there were no bulls to be found anywhere.  Copper’s price fell away with such undignified haste that it made that US$9000/t level look like a mirage: US$8415/t ($3.82/lb) on that 19<sup>th</sup> , a loss of $366/t since the prior trading day Friday, another $150/t down on the third trading Wednesday of the month, the 21<sup>st</sup> .  Thereafter, only daily falls in chunks of US$400-500/t seemed good enough for the red metal: US$7700/t ($3.49/

lb) on Thursday 22nd , and the week’s close at US$7290/t ($3.31/lb) on the 23rd . If anyone thought they had had their fill of grim reading, they found the storyline over that weekend had not changed. After moving below the US$7000/t level ($3.17/lb) during intra-day trading on Monday 26th , that day’s closing price drop of $40/t brought a challenge to the US$7250/t level ($3.29/lb) sharply into view, leaving copper markets asking what the new reality was for the metal and where it would head next. **..as did all metals** If copper needs to look for any consolation, it should not feel alone in being entirely rejected. However, it might still consider itself “singled out” for almost the harshest treatment. Since the last trading day of August and through to the 26th , copper lost roughly 23% of its cash price. Lead even worse, at 26%. Nickel comes somewhat close to copper at around 17%, with zinc not so far behind at 16%. Aluminium got off the lightest with only a 9.6% decline which is not surprising given that prices were already close to its marginal cost of production, while tin has been the only metal whose price has increased during the month. Investors have clearly shied away from risk as regional economies and their varied degrees of weakness have pushed them to the safer havens of cash and government bonds. #### **Copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 1800 10000

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - September 2011 Page 3 of 22 Copper Monthly Update **Copper market remains in deficit** It is true that the near-term market fundamentals for copper have weakened a little since our last report. In August, we were showing a metal stock draw down of 350kt for this year, and now this figure stands at just under 220kt, with the shift being shared almost equally between lower global demand (-74kt) and higher supply (+60kt). This has had the effect of raising stock days of consumption from our 45 day figure of a month ago to 50, but this still remains well below historical averages. But these are modest changes. In essence, copper’s price bruise came at the hands of a macro-economic beating with market makers punishing political inertia, resulting in an en masse flight of capital away from commodities and other riskier investments into the traditional safe havens noted earlier. However, given the sizeable fall in copper prices in recent weeks, we must look for some measure of repair here first. **Premia changes everywhere – but not for the usual logical reasons** In the meantime, copper’s immediate responses at the micro-level have been mixed. In the US,

where business levels in July were truly awful and August’s were only marginally better, premia fell away to 4.75-5.50 cents/lb in most regions, although the northeast still sees 5.56.0c/lb or so. In this way, the premia changes reflect the bearish trading conditions. But the same cannot be said in China. There, a positive arb is encouraging imports along with rising premia – to $120-140/t, and even higher ($150/t) more recently in some cases (see pages 7-8) – but these superficially bullish conditions are not a direct reflection of improved rates of business but mirror the tightening credit situation faced by market players needing to hold more collateral. In this case, the “collateral” is physical copper metal stock. Equally, the dramatic increase in cancelled warrants held in Korean LME warehouses since mid-month will likely be material headed for China, given the favourable arbitrage between the LME and SHFE and the improvement in Chinese premia. Meanwhile, European activity remains stuck in summer lull mode, and premia have edged downwards by $10/t or so for Grade A and Chilean material. **There is a silver lining to copper’s new price level** Arguably, there is a silver lining to this month’s collapse in the copper price. For many months, the skeptics have pointed to the differential between the prices of copper and the red metal’s closest competitor, aluminium, and have been looking for an en masse switch across to the lighter metal. These discussions will now not be heard again for the rest of this year at least. Secondly, scrap markets have made hay during these times of US$9000-10000/t copper. But now those segments of the manufacturing sectors which can use significant amounts of scrap will soon find that their preferred material has dried up - if they have not found that out already - and they will have to turn to primary metal. For wider stability, of course, all markets will need to feel reassured that the various European, Japanese and US governments are re-gaining some control over debt issues. And our view is that this will come through during this final quarter even if only in sentiment rather than any physical reality. But should this sentiment prompt renewed confidence, copper’s existing sound fundamentals will prevent further sustained challenges to the downside. Our revised Q4 average price forecast of US$8400/t ($3.81/lb) reflects our belief that copper will rebound from this month’s losses, and indeed move further up during H1 2012 while the mild physical market deficit remains in place. From then on, though, the game changes, and a surge in new mine supply through to 2014 and even in to 2015 will bring downward pressure to bear on copper quotes once again. #### **Price forecasts and world quarterly supply/demand balance – (kt)** |||**Refined**

## Consumption 

Movements in both commodity and equity markets have been dramatic over the past month but the extent of real impact on end use demand remains to be seen.  We had always forecast a slowdown in demand in the second half of the year, although we have toned this down further since our last monthly report and now expect global growth of 4.6% this year. The outlook for 2012 is far from certain but overall growth will undoubtedly be supported by continued strength in the Chinese market.  Even if the global economy were to enter a double-dip recession, thereby easing inflationary concerns, China would then be able to turn the liquidity tap back on to reinvigorate its own market and support consumption. 

### **Europe and CIS** 

**Euro debt issues paint a bleak backdrop** The ongoing euro debt crisis continues to rumble on, with particularly dramatic effects seen in the stock markets this month.  Although movements in equity prices have very little real impact on the average man in the street, the negative headlines that they generate does have a psychological impact, with this often resulting in a less positive approach to spending.  This can then feed through into real effects on economic activity. The lags in economic data do not allow us to evaluate this as yet, although industrial activity has already started to slow in any case, with negative sentiment adding further downside risk. 

**FY demand in Western Europe to be flat** We have kept our forecasts for Western Europe broadly in line with last month and will reiterate our expectation of no growth in regional demand this year.  Although we do expect improvement in demand next year, the outlook here too is clouded by the ongoing debt crisis. 

**Premia edge lower** Premia had moved lower over the course of the past month amid sluggish demand for material. Semis producers are certainly taking a cautious view on placing orders, although this has bee

n the case for some time anyway, so this does not account for all of the weakness. We understand that firms are holding off placing orders as much as they might have otherwise in a bid to gain more favourable terms in annual negotiations. **Italian semis output slips in Q2** It is not possible to say the extent of the real impact on demand from the ongoing European debt crisis in general and in Italy in particular but whatever the cause, Italian semis production fell in the second quarter. Output of copper semis slipped 4.9%, while copper alloy semis production contracted by a lesser 1% to leave total copper and copper alloy semis down by 3.1% overall, compared to a 1% expansion in the first quarter. Key sector wire was a notable underperformer, falling by 6.1% year on year, mirroring the declines in output at Aurubis that we discussed last month. #### **Italian copper semis production – (kt)** 40 360

**Fourth straight year of contraction in Eurozone construction** Our forecast fall of 0.7% this year would take total construction investment to €740Bn (in 2000 prices), 15% below its 2007 peak. However, activity is not falling across all countries. Total construction is likely to increase in Germany, France and Italy in 2011, although not by enough to offset the ongoing slump in Spain – where building is forecast to drop by a further 9%. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - September 2011 Page 5 of 22 Copper Monthly Update The residential construction sector was significantly affected by recession in Europe, with housing investment down by almost 20% between 2007 and 2010. However, the residential sector is now leading the recovery with activity increasing by 1.8% year-on-year through the first half of 2011 – led by 6% annual growth in Germany. We expect Eurozone residential construction growth to accelerate slightly from 1.5% in 2011 to 1.8% in 2012, as recovery spreads from the core to the periphery. Of course, further worsening of the Eurozone sovereign debt crisis would lead to a further tightening of credit markets, and this would likely cause a further slump in residential construction. While we expect recovery to begin in the Eurozone residential housing sector this year, the same cannot be said of the commercial and public construction sectors. The tightening of fiscal policy across the majority of the region is currently and will continue to delay public investments in construction, especially in central and southern Europe. Commercial building activity is showing signs of growth in Germany and some other core Eurozone economies, but construction is being hampered by lacklustre economic recovery, w

ith businesses seeing little incentive to invest when capacity is already ample. Wood Mackenzie forecasts non-residential construction to fall by 2.7% in 2011 and 2.3% in 2012. As a result, we do not expect growth in total construction to return until 2013 at the earliest. ### **Americas** **US copper endures traditional summer demand drop** In line with the usual patterns of prior years, US copper demand was encouragingly strong during the first four months of this year, cooled down somewhat in months five to six, and then seemed to disappear for the month of July. While the US economy appeared to be improving during the earlier months of the year, copper demand also benefited and remained pretty healthy, especially in the wire markets. But following the renewed discussion over the wider global economic downturn which started in May, the previous hesitation seen at the buying level has worsened to a halt. After showing 14 month-on-month improvements out of 15 during the February 2010-April 2011 period, total US wire rod shipments, according to data from the American Bureau of Metal Statistics (ABMS), contracted in July for the third straight month. As noted, July is indeed traditionally weak, but the 14% drop in both shipments and production this July compared to the same month in 2010 illustrates just how lifeless the market seems to be. This was, in fact, the worst monthly fall since Q4 2009. Furthermore, ABMS data show that rod held in stock grew to 31.3kt this July, from 28.6kt a month prior and from July 2010’s 23.8kt. **..but some improvement noted in August** Preliminary data for August showed a return to June levels of both production and shipments, and so at least there was no further decline from July. Even so, production, at 105.5kt, was still 4% down on August 2010 rates, while shipments of 108.8kt were a marginal 0.7% down year on year. Some macro economic data offered little encouragement either: sales of new homes in August, for example, fell by 2.3% and represented the fourth consecutive decline and a six-month low. #### **US wire rod production and shipments– (kt)** 150

**But Russian material continues to flood in** That said, domestic rod producers, despite having reduced their output schedules to match sales, are also continuing to face high imports from Russia.  These came about from May, largely entering Baltimore and New Orleans ports, and have been the direct consequence of the Russian government placing an export tax on cathode from last December.  The cathodes have remained at home to be converted domestically, then exported as rod, tariff-free.  Russian rod producers began by exporting to southern Europe, then turned to what at the time, back in May, were resurgent rod markets in the USA.  For the months of May and June, a combined total of 7.05kt of rod came into the USA from Russia, but in July alone a further 8kt came in.  American traders and distributors have clearly absorbed the lower-priced Russian imports, leaving US rod producers to respond in the only manner possible in the short term, which has been to reduce output themselves.  So far, there is no talk publicly of the domestics heading for protectionist measures from Washington D.C., but should the market not pick up noticeably into the fourth quarter, we would expect to see some action by the mills in order to protect what should be the typically strongest period in 2012. 

**Mueller Industries suffers plant fire at Wynne, and Hussey files for Chapter 11** Aside from the fireworks over copper prices on the global stage, the US copper sector endured shocks of its own at both ends of this month.  On the 7<sup>th</sup> , Mueller Industries Corp acknowledged that a fire at its Wynne, AR tube plant had damaged the copper casting equipment, as well as the areas used for PVC plastic fittings for DWV applications and fabrication of line sets for air conditioning applications.  The company immediately laid off 170 out of 465 employees, and said that orders would be fulfilled from its other plants, which we believe will include Fulton, MS, and would also turn to third parties for other sourcing.  Although the damage will be covered by insurance, Mueller has yet to indicate whether or not it will re-build at Wynne.  According to the International Copper Study Group, Wynne has a copper melting capacity of between 60120kt/a; it was formerly owned by Halstead up to the 1990s. 

And toward the end of the month, on the 27<sup>th</sup> , fabricated products maker Hussey Copper filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings, citing the volatility of copper prices as the main cause for its financial distress.  Formed in 1848 and based in Leetsdale, PA, Hussey also claims to hold a 70% share of the US electrical bus bar market and to be the “leading bus bar producer in the world” courtesy of output at its Eminence, KY facility.  Court documents show that Hussey has debts of $38.2M with first-lien financial institutions such as Wells Fargo, Bank of America and PNC Bank, and $2.4M to second-lien lender,

Schneider Electric SA.  It also owes $29M in unsecured trade debt primarily to suppliers of copper and other metals, with $9.05M of this being claimed by Metal Management Pittsburgh of Elizabeth, PA, $2.7M by CMC Recycling of Irving, TX, and $2.6M to HKP Metals of McKeesport, PA.  According to press reports, Hussey has agreed to be taken over by stalking horse bidder KHC Acquisition LLC of Red Bank, NJ, after attempts to renegotiate its debts failed, but there will be a bidding process to find other possible suitors willing to pay more than KHC’s as yet undisclosed offer. 

### **China** 

**Industrial activity eases back as inflation begins to edge lower** The latest release of industrial production data revealed that activity has slowed modestly in line with authorities’ aims to slow price inflation.  Engineering a soft landing is easier said than done but price increases have begun to slow, with the latest figures showing CPI up by 6.2% in August after hitting 6.5% the previous month.  One swallow doesn’t make a summer of course but this decline fits with our view of easing inflation in the final part of the year.  Controlling prices is the easy part but controlling prices without slowing industrial activity too sharply is more difficult.  However, August’s 13.5% hike in industrial production is broadly in line with our view of full year IP growth.  Overall, data releases suggest an end to the tightening cycle in China, particularly when set against the backdrop of concerns over the health of major economies in Europe and North America. 

**Demand slows into the final quarter** Order books at semis producers would typically turn higher in September, although there is a lot less activity this month amid tight credit conditions and concern over the economic outlook. Fabricators are taking a cautious view of inventory levels even if there has been some modest increases in a bid to take advantage of lower prices.  That said, we maintain a bullish view overall for copper demand in China, although with a slightly softer than previously expected fourth quarter, we now expect demand to grow by 8% for the full year. 

**China imports continue to climb** Imports of refined copper have continued to recover, with the latest shipments for August revealing a 21% increase on the prior month, although this still represented a 12.5% year-on-year fall.  Imports have gained every month since June, lifted by favourable arbitrage conditions between the LME and SHFE.  We expect that imports will remain on average above 200kt per month through the remainder of the year. 

That imports have continued to increase would normally be considered as indicating strong demand for refined copper, although we understand that increasingly tight credit conditions are causing firms to turn to copper as a vehicle to raise cash against.  This is significant for a number of reasons but the collapse in copper prices over the past month adds an extra dimension.  If copper is being hel

d as collateral against a loan and the value of that collateral diminishes then the borrower effectively has a margin call on that loan and has to supply more collateral.  That is, they need more copper, which in part explains the increase in bonded warehouse stocks this month.  If firms are unable to meet the requirement for extra collateral they are effectively defaulting on their loan, which is then being cancelled by banks.

The rise in premia this month to $120-140/t and even as high as $150/t on occasion would suggest that rather than loans being cancelled firms have been able to post collateral up to now and those chasing after material to do so has lifted premia. 

**Stocks edge higher overall** Stocks held in SHFE registered warehouses have remained broadly flat this month, although as we noted above, those in bonded stocks have increased to around 400kt from around 300kt at the end of August.  Typically, an increase in stocks levels should be viewed negatively for demand, although if it is the case the material is being tied up in financing deals then we do not consider this increase to be reflective of weak demand as such.  However, underlying demand is slowing. 

**Mixed picture for transport sector** Automotive production increased by 9% year on year in August, while production in the first 8 months of the year was up by 4.7% compared to the same period of last year.  The sustainability of this upturn is unclear however considering the strong output of the last quarter of 2010.  Recovering auto production in both China and Japan recently should encourage restocking by auto part makers, which in turn should increase demand for connector strip and magnet wire for wiring harnesses. 

However, on a weaker note, total fixed asset investment in the railway industry fell by 1.5% in the first 7 months of the year. The railway ministry announced in May that rail construction investment this year would be 600 billion yuan, down from an earlier estimate of 700 billion yuan.  However, investment could even fall below this level because the Chinese government has ordered a temporary halt on approving new railway lines and urged a thorough overhaul of the country's high-speed railways following a train collision in July.  The slow development of the railway industry will reduce demand for railway power and signal cable and other related copper containing products in this sector. 

**Construction building up steam** Construction activity in China continues to expand at a rapid pace as rising incomes and urbanisation boost demand for higher quality housing and commercial real estate.  At the start of 2011, many commentators were concerned that the rapid rise in construction activity in recent years had resulted in an oversupply of housing and commercial space, which would flood the market and depress demand for new construction in the years ahead.  To d

ate, these concerns appear unfounded, with construction growth accelerating in all sectors bar infrastructure throughout 2011. ### **Japan** 

**Industrial output running out of steam?** The initial pace of economic recovery in Japan caught us by surprise, with industrial output surging back to life after the interruptions caused by the March disaster.  However, the bad news is that following the sharp month-on-month gains of May and June, the recovery seems to be running out of steam.  Indeed, industrial production climbed less than 1% month on month in July and is still below last year’s level of output by 1.5%. We do, however, still expect output to climb into positive territory on a year-on-year basis by the final quarter of this year, in particular buoyed by the recovery of the automotive sector, which accounts for a significant portion of industrial activity in Japan. 

**Mixed picture for August shipments** Wire and cable shipments enjoyed a recovery in August after the slide of the prior month, amid hopes the July figure was simply a blip amid an upward trend.  Certainly, the 1.3% year-on-year increase was to be welcomed, while it is also noteworthy that shipments only fell modestly on a month-on-month basis when they would typically be expected to fall more sharply owing to holidays in mid-August.  On a more negative note, however, brass mill shipments performed less well, falling by over 4% in July, and are now down by 1.8% in the year to date.  Wire and cable shipments on the other hand are down by only 0.4% in the first eight months of the year. 

**Construction building up speed?** As we have noted previously, it was the relative strength of the construction sector that cushioned what otherwise would have been a sharp decline in shipments overall.  A combination of real demand from the reconstruction of temporary homes in addition to stock-building through the supply chain in anticipation of increased demand resulted in shipments of wire and cable rising by 15% year on year in the second quarter.  Meanwhile, there has also been an improvement in housing starts over the past couple of months, with starts recording their highest level this year in June, which was followed up by a 21.2% year-on-year increase in July.  It is too early to say if this is the start of a trend of increased activity or indeed whether this is simply related to reconstruction works getting underway. 

**Automotive market recovery continues apace** The recovery of the automotive market mirrors the fast pace of industrial output in general, with production increasing sharply in May and June from its nadir in April but the pace slowing in July.  Production remains in negative territory on a year-on-year basis although expectations are that automakers will be back to full rates of output by the end of September.  This bodes well for an improvement in wire and cable shipments to the sector, which collapsed in Q2, sliding some 35% year-on-year.  As with production of vehicles, shipments have enjoyed month-on-month increases

since May and with car makers planning to hire extra workers in autumn in an attempt to recover lost ground, this sector should be supportive to refined copper demand in the final part of the year. We expect auto production to rebound solidly in 2012, which augurs well for further gains in consumption of cathode also. able and Chinese smelters turned to scrap processing because the substantial discounts available in the No.2 market meant that this material could be purchased and consumed profitably. On paper, copper in concentrate supplies are likely to rise faster than primary smelting capacity in 2012 and on this basis we would expect average global smelter utilisation rates to increase marginally, from an estimated level of 82.2% this year to 83.4% next year, against an optimal level of 88% and at the expense of lowering concentrate stocks further towards the 30 days of consumption mark. **Teck moves ahead with HVC investments…** Teck Resources t

his month outlined a $475M expenditure at its Highland Valley Copper operation in British Columbia, Canada, which guarantees production through to 2025.  Prior to this announcement, HVC was scheduled for closure in 2019, but not because of a lack of in-ground resources.  The 40-year old mill has been showing its age for some years, with actual production rates falling through inefficiencies (as well as pit wall and ore grade issues) and an increasing cost profile.  Following a near three-year review, Teck intends to reverse that decline with this investment, which will see a complete replacement of the existing copper and molybdenum bulk flotation complex.  Management hopes this will result in 10% higher throughputs and a 2% improvement in copper recovery.  Construction will begin this quarter and will be completed by the end of 2013.  Last year, HVC produced 98.5kt of copper in concentrate, down from 2009’s 118.2kt, and guidance issued in this year’s Q2 statement indicated full-year output would be lower still at 95kt due to poorer ore grades being available.  In 2010, geotechnical issues in the Valley pit area of the mine forced a need for pit wall push backs at both east and west walls costing $48M, and this project will only be completed later this year. 

**..but struggles with negotiations for a new labour contract** On the face of it, this announcement of ongoing investment at HVC could not have come at a better time, as far as labour relations are concerned.  The current five-year labour agreement ends on the 30<sup>th</sup> of this month, but if the company was hoping that its recent decision to extend the operation’s life would bring about a prompt renewal in the talks with the 1030-strong United Steelworkers Local 7619, it looks like being disappointed.  As of the 22<sup>nd</sup> of this month, after several weeks of negotiations, the two sides remained sufficiently far apart for Teck to request the involvement of a mediator.  The Local claims that the three major issues of wages, benefits and pensions have not even been discussed properly.  Equally, it claims that Teck wants to “gut” the copper bonus, which was introduced in 2003 (when prices _averaged_ 80.7c/lb) and which kicks in at a level of 1% when prices exceed C$1.22/lb (which they have done, by and large, since February 2004) and reaches a maximum of 6% if prices exceed C$1.27/lb.  The Local says it did well out of the 2006 round, with 4% basic salary increments each year across all grades, amongst other improvements, and, given available bullish copper price forecasts, it believes it should do better this time.  The company will point to the sharp drop in copper prices this month alone to illustrate the precarious nature of promising what cannot be guaranteed.  Given the apparent distance between the two sides, a strike vote took place on September 25<sup>th</sup> and obtained an overwhelming majority 99.5% in favour of recommending such action by the Local leadership should

the September 30<sup>th</sup> deadline come and go without a binding agreement with Teck.  From October 1<sup>st</sup> , then, it appears that the Union might strike for what would be only the third time in its 43-year history. Unfortunately, those two occasions offer little by way of how this third strike will go: in 1972 the action lasted for two weeks only, but in 1989 it went on for 107 days.

**Rio, Anglo intend to exit Palabora** Citing the limitations of its size, Rio Tinto and Anglo American signalled their intent early September to sell their interests in Palabora Mining Co in South Africa at the earliest opportunity.  In its heyday, the integrated mine through to copper rod producer had produced as much as 139kt cathode, but has averaged under 70kt over the three most recent years, with various reasons impeding production levels.  The mine currently has sufficient resources out to early 2016, but despite there being a possibility that the ongoing feasibility study into extending mine-life to 2030, the two partners believe it will not leave Palabora with sufficient scale to fit in with their wider copper operations’ profiles.  Equally, the possibility of mining and processing the on-site magnetite resources is outside both companies’ areas of focus.  The likely valuation for the combined 74.5% stakes held by the two majors is around US$730M. 

**Rio pushes ahead with Eagle** Rio Tinto subsidiary, Kennecott Eagle Minerals Co (KEMC), has received a green light from a local Michigan court to build an underground entryway to its proposed Eagle nickel-copper mine in the state’s Upper Peninsula.  This most recent permission, gained mid-month, should allow KEMC to substantially complete the mine and bring it into production by 2013, given that surface facilities at the mine site itself are almost finished. Explorations teams from Rio Tinto discovered Eagle in 2002, and have identified a 4.1Mt resource assaying 3.6% Ni and 2.9% Cu.  The company plans to utilise stop-hole mining methods to extract 16kt/a nickel in concentrate and 10kt/a copper in concentrate over a seven- to eight-year mine life.  Ore from Eagle will be trucked to a previously operating iron ore crushing and concentrating mill at Humboldt, 70km to the south.  Kennecott bought the facility in September 2008, and plans to spend US$80M there to bring it up to suitable requirements.  Nickel concentrate is likely to assay 13% and will be processed in Canada, while the copper concentrate will grade close to 30% Cu.  KEMC had hoped to commission the mine back in 2009, but it has had to face up to several legal challenges from anti-mining groups concerned about waste water and air emissions. 

**Zambia goes with Sata** Despite having overseen the most dramatic expansion of copper production facilities in recent decades, Zambian President Rupiah Banda lost to Michael Sata’s Patriotic Front p

arty after his Movement for Multiparty Democracy had ruled the country for 20 years.  This is the fourth time lucky for Sata, following defeats in 2001, 2006 and 2008.  During the last campaign, part of Sata’s platform focused on his disapproval of the foreign investment that had flooded into the country in recent years, namely from China, especially regarding labour conditions.  This time around, he significantly toned down that rhetoric.  Even so, observers believe there will be changes ahead for the mining sector. One of the first actions to be re-visited could be a re-imposition of a tax on mining company profits.  Former President Banda scrapped the 25% tax rate previously prevailing, and Sata has pledged to reinstate a tax, even if it is not at that level.  Secondly, under former President Levy Mwanamasa, the Citizens Economic Empowerment Act – a Zambian equivalent of the RSA Black Economic Empowerment (BEE) – was written into law, but upon his untimely death in 2008 the new President Banda decided against implementing the law.  Sata may well push that agenda again.  Further into his term, Sata could embark on reforms of capital markets and the taxation system to reverse what are widely seen as advantages favouring well-funded foreign investors over nationals who cannot obtain similar access to capital. 

**Kazzinc commissions smelter/refinery** Glencore’s 50.7%-held subsidiary, Kazzinc, reports that it has completed commissioning work at its copper smelter and refinery at Ust-Kamenogorsk in eastern Kazakhstan, and this will now allow locally produced concentrate to be processed through to cathode.  To date, Kazzinc has sold its concentrate to third parties, but this has been hampered this year due to unfavourable spot TCRCs in China following the earthquake and tsunami in Japan.  Kazzinc built up a stock of copper concentrate in the first half of the year valued at US$127M, but this material will now be processed through its new smelter/refinery complex.  We expect c.20kt of refined cathode to become available through the complex this year, building to 65kt in 2012 and topping out at 70kt from 2013.  However, Kazzinc is already considering a further expansion to 87.5kt in the long term.
